{{Short description|Theorem in complex analysis}}
[[Image:Runge theorem.svg|right|thumb|Given a holomorphic function ''f'' on the blue compact set and a point in each of the holes, one can approximate ''f'' as well as desired by rational functions having poles only at those three points.]]

In [[complex analysis]], '''Runge's theorem''' (also known as '''Runge's approximation theorem''') is named after the German mathematician [[Carl Runge]] who first proved it in 1885.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Runge |first=C. |date=1885-12-01 |title=Zur Theorie der Eindeutigen Analytischen Functionen |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02400416 |journal=Acta Mathematica |language=de |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=229–244 |doi=10.1007/BF02400416 |issn=1871-2509|url-access=subscription }}</ref> It states the following:

Denoting by '''C''' the set of [[complex numbers]], let ''K'' be a closed subset of '''<math>\mathbb C \cup\{\infty\}</math>''' and let ''f'' be a [[function (mathematics)|function]] which is [[holomorphic function|holomorphic]] on an [[open set]] containing ''K''. If ''A'' is a set containing [[Existential quantification|at least one]] complex number from every [[connected set|connected component]] of <math>\mathbb C \cup\{\infty\} \setminus K</math>, then there exists a [[sequence]] <math>(r_n)_{n\in\N}</math> of [[rational function]]s which [[uniform convergence|converges uniformly]] to ''f'' on ''K'' and such that all the [[pole (complex analysis)|poles]] of the functions <math>(r_n)_{n\in\N}</math> are in ''A.''

Note that not every complex number in ''A'' needs to be a pole of every rational function of the sequence <math>(r_n)_{n\in\N}</math>. We merely know that for all members of <math>(r_n)_{n\in\N}</math> that '''do''' have poles, those poles lie in ''A''.

One aspect that makes this theorem so powerful is that one can choose the set ''A'' arbitrarily. In other words, one can choose '''any''' complex numbers from the bounded connected components of <math>\mathbb C \cup\{\infty\} \setminus K</math> and the theorem guarantees the existence of a sequence of rational functions with poles only amongst those chosen numbers.

For the special case in which ''K'' is a compact subset of <math>\mathbb C</math> and <math>\mathbb C \setminus K</math> is a connected set one can pick <math>A = \{\infty\}</math>. Since rational functions with no poles except at infinity are simply [[polynomial]]s, we get the following [[corollary]]: If ''K'' is a compact subset of '''C''' such that '''C'''\''K'' is a connected set, and ''f'' is a holomorphic function on an open set containing  ''K'', then there exists a sequence of polynomials <math>(p_n)</math> that approaches ''f'' uniformly on ''K''.

==Sketch of proof==
An [[elementary proof]], inspired by {{harvtxt|Sarason|1998}}, proceeds as follows. There is a closed piecewise-linear contour Γ in the open set, containing ''K'' in its interior, such that all the chosen distinguished points are in its exterior. By [[Cauchy's integral formula]]

:<math>f(w)={1\over 2\pi i} \int_\Gamma {f(z) \, dz\over z-w}</math>

for ''w'' in ''K''. Riemann approximating sums can be used to approximate the contour integral uniformly over ''K'' (there is a similar formula for the derivative). Each term in the sum is a scalar multiple of (''z'' − ''w'')<sup>−1</sup> for some point ''z'' on the contour. This gives a uniform approximation by a rational function with poles on Γ.

To modify this to an approximation with poles at specified points in each component of the complement of ''K'', it is enough to check this for terms of the form  (''z''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''w'')<sup>−1</sup>. If ''z''<sub>0</sub> is the point in the same component as ''z'', take a path from ''z'' to  ''z''<sub>0</sub>.

If two points are sufficiently close on the path, we may use the formula
:<math>\frac{1}{z - z_0} = \frac{1}{z - w_0} \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left( \frac{z_0 - w_0}{z - w_0} \right)^n</math> (verified by [[geometric series]])
valid on the circle-complement <math>|z_0 - w_0| < |z - w|</math>; note that the chosen path has a positive distance to K by compactness. That series can be truncated to give a rational function with poles only at the second point uniformly close to the original function on ''K''. Proceeding by steps along the path from ''z'' to ''z''<sub>0</sub> the original function (''z'' − ''w'')<sup>−1</sup> can be successively modified to give a rational function with poles only at ''z''<sub>0</sub>.

If ''z''<sub>0</sub> is the [[point at infinity]], then by the above procedure the rational function  (''z'' − ''w'')<sup>−1</sup> can first be approximated by a rational function ''g'' with poles at ''R'' > 0 where ''R'' is so large that ''K'' lies in ''w'' < ''R''.  The [[Taylor series]] expansion of ''g'' about 0 can then be truncated to give a polynomial approximation on ''K''.

== Generalizations ==
When <math>K</math> is a compact subset of the [[complex plane]] <math>\mathbb C</math> such that <math>\mathbb C \setminus K</math> is connected, [[Mergelyan's theorem]] relaxes the condition on <math>f</math>. Instead of requiring <math>f</math> to be holomorphic on an open set containing <math>K</math>, it only requires <math>f</math> to be continuous on <math>K</math>, and holomorphic on the interior of <math>K</math>.

Runge's theorem generalizes to [[Riemann surface]]s.<ref>{{Citation |last=Fornæss |first=John Erik |chapter=Holomorphic Approximation: The Legacy of Weierstrass, Runge, Oka–Weil, and Mergelyan |date=2020 |title=Advancements in Complex Analysis: From Theory to Practice |pages=133–192 |editor-last=Breaz |editor-first=Daniel |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-40120-7_5 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-40120-7_5 |isbn=978-3-030-40120-7 |last2=Forstnerič |first2=Franc |last3=Wold |first3=Erlend F. |editor2-last=Rassias |editor2-first=Michael Th.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>{{Reference page|location=Theorem 4}}

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem|note=|math_statement= If <math display="inline">K</math> is a compact set in a Riemann surface <math display="inline">X</math>, then every holomorphic function <math display="inline">f</math> on a neighborhood of <math display="inline">K</math> can be approximated uniformly on <math display="inline">K</math> by meromorphic functions <math display="inline">F</math> on <math display="inline">X</math> without poles in <math display="inline">K</math>, and by holomorphic functions on <math display="inline">X</math> if <math display="inline">X \backslash K</math> has no connected components relatively compact in <math display="inline">X</math>.
}}

The original Runge's theorem is obtained by setting <math>X = \mathbb C \cup\{\infty\} \setminus A</math>, where <math>A</math> contains one element per connected component of <math>\mathbb C \cup\{\infty\} \setminus K</math>.

For functions of several complex variables, a naive generalization of Runge's theorem is false. Further restrictions are necessary to make analogous theorems that are true. One generalization is the [[Oka–Weil theorem]].

=== Runge domain ===
We say that an open subset <math>U</math> of <math>X</math> is a '''Runge subset''' if any holomorphic function on <math>U</math> is the [[limit of a sequence]] of global holomorphic functions on <math>X</math> in the [[compact-open topology]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Forstnerič |first=F. |last2=Kutzschebauch |first2=F. |date=2022-06-01 |title=The First Thirty Years of Andersén-Lempert Theory |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10476-022-0130-1 |journal=Analysis Mathematica |language=en |volume=48 |issue=2 |pages=489–544 |doi=10.1007/s10476-022-0130-1 |issn=1588-273X|arxiv=2111.08802 }}</ref>
